# May 2026 Labor Market Update: What employers and job seekers should know

The May jobs report delivered a stronger-than-expected result, showing U.S. employers added 172,000 jobs, according to the Bureau of Labor Statistics (BLS). That figure is well above economists’ projections and marks the first time since early 2024 that the economy has seen 3 consecutive months of job gains above 100,000. The BLS also revised March and April payrolls higher by a combined 93,000 jobs.

Those numbers point to a labor market that has remained resilient despite ongoing economic uncertainty and market volatility. However, the recent pattern of job growth doesn’t erase the persistent hiring challenges many organizations face, including small and midsize firms. # U.S. Jobs Surge Signals Labor Market Resilience, But Risks Linger

By Emily Chen / June 13, 2026 

The U.S. labor market’s latest jobs report signals a genuine shift from the sluggishness that defined much of 2023, yet it arrives with a warning: resilience is not synonymous with comfort. Nonfarm payrolls surged by 172,000 in May, crushing the consensus expectation of 105,000 and extending a three-month streak of gains above 100,000—a pattern unseen since early 2024. The unemployment rate held at 4.3%, and revisions to March and April data added a combined 93,000 jobs, lifting the three-month average to 188,000. This is not a boom, but it is a marked improvement over last year’s near-stagnation, when monthly job growth hovered below 10,000.

# US employers added 172,000 jobs in May, but health care and government drove nearly all the gains

 David Keller 4 months ago 4 months ago 0 9 mins 

 DC Studio/Freepik

American workers looking for jobs outside health care and government got little encouragement from the May 2026 employment report. Total nonfarm payroll employment increased by 172,000, and the unemployment rate held at 4.3 percent, but the gains were sharply concentrated in a handful of publicly funded or demographically driven sectors. For hiring managers and job seekers in manufacturing, retail, and professional services, the headline number masked a much thinner labor market.
